Chapter 1 check: densities, identically distributed, and the whole chapter

One sitting, about 30 minutes. No reading today. Two short re-teaches (about 11 minutes), then the check across all six sections of Chapter 1 and one proof (about 20 minutes). Two wins: build a density whose value is bigger than 1; say what "identically distributed" requires and what it doesn't.

Why this lesson

Chapter 2 starts from Chapter 1's objects: random variables, their cdfs and their densities. Before we build on them, this page checks that the whole chapter is there, including §1.1 on sets, which the pretest let us skip. Two ideas haven't fully landed yet, so they come first: what a density's value can be, and what "identically distributed" promises.

No reading today. This is a check, so everything on it comes from Chapter 1 sections you've already read. If something doesn't come back, look at the explanation after you answer, then reread that section of Casella & Berger.

Number boxes take expressions: type * for ×, /, ^ for powers, sqrt( ), exp( ) and choose(n, k). When you get one right, say honestly whether you knew it or guessed.

Part 1 · Build a density taller than 1 (re-teach, about 6 minutes)

From the reading (§1.6), with examples beyond it. Earlier we said a density can be larger than 1. This time you build one yourself.

Recap: what makes a function a pdf (Casella & Berger, Theorem 1.6.5). \(f\) is a pdf exactly when (a) \(f(x) \ge 0\) for every \(x\), and (b) the total area \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x)\,dx\) is 1. Probabilities are areas: \(P(a < X \le b) = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\). Nothing in (a) or (b) puts a ceiling on \(f(x)\).

Squeeze the interval. \(X\) is uniform on \([0, w]\): its density is a flat rectangle of height \(h\) on that interval and 0 elsewhere. Condition (b) says the rectangle's area is 1, so \(h \cdot w = 1\) and \(h = 1/w\).

Watch the height. \(w = 2\) gives \(h = 0.5\). \(w = 1\) gives \(h = 1\). What happens as \(w\) shrinks below 1? Try it before the next question.

\(X\) is uniform on \([0, w]\) (a flat density on that interval, 0 elsewhere). What width \(w\) makes \(f(0.4) = 1.5\)? (A fraction is fine. Your \(w\) must be bigger than 0.4, so that 0.4 is inside the interval.)

Height \(= 1/w = 1.5\) gives \(w = \tfrac23\), which is bigger than 0.4. So uniform on \([0, \tfrac23]\) is a legitimate pdf (area \(1.5 \times \tfrac23 = 1\)) with \(f(0.4) = 1.5\), and it's continuous at 0.4.

What can't go above 1. Any area under \(f\): on \([0, \tfrac23]\) with \(h = 1.5\), \(P(0.4 < X \le 0.41) = 1.5 \times 0.01 = 0.015\), and the area over the whole interval is exactly 1. The narrower the interval, the taller the rectangle (\(w = 0.1\) needs \(h = 10\)). The value \(f(x)\) is probability per unit length; areas are probabilities.

Why textbooks say "f is continuous at x" before using f(x). Changing \(f\) at a single point changes no area, so it changes no probability. A single value \(f(x)\) only means something where \(f\) is continuous; there, a short interval around \(x\) has probability close to \(f(x) \times\) length. Continuity is about which value to trust; it puts no limit on how big it is.

Say it this way: "A density can take any value 0 or above; only areas under it are probabilities, and those are at most 1." Not this: "A pdf's value is at most 1."

Not every density is flat. \(f(x) = c\,x(1 - x)\) for \(0 \le x \le 1\) and 0 elsewhere. Find the constant \(c\) that makes \(f\) a pdf, then give \(f(\tfrac12)\). (An expression is fine.)

\(\int_0^1 x(1 - x)\,dx = \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac16\), so \(c = 6\). Then \(f(\tfrac12) = 6 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = 1.5\): a smooth, continuous density whose peak is 1.5. (This is the Beta(2, 2) distribution, which you'll meet in Chapter 3.)

\(X\) has density \(f(x) = c\,x\) for \(0 \le x \le \tfrac12\) and 0 elsewhere. First find the constant \(c\) that makes \(f\) a pdf, then give \(f(0.4)\). (An expression is fine.)

Area \(= \int_0^{1/2} c\,x\,dx = c \cdot \tfrac18 = 1\), so \(c = 8\). Then \(f(0.4) = 8 \times 0.4 = 3.2\). The density is continuous at 0.4, so 3.2 is a meaningful value, and it's above 1.

\(X\) is a random variable and \(a < b\) are numbers. Which of these can be greater than 1?

A pmf value is \(P(X = x)\), a cdf value is \(P(X \le x)\), and \(P(a < X \le b)\) is a probability too: all three lie in \([0, 1]\). A pdf value is a density, so it can be any nonnegative number (uniform on \([0, 0.1]\) has density 10).

Part 2 · Identically distributed: same probabilities, not same outcomes (re-teach, about 5 minutes)

From the reading (§1.5). Two things to fix: identically distributed variables can agree on some outcomes (they just don't have to), and "same cdf" means equal at every \(x\), not at one.

Recap: Definition 1.5.8 and Theorem 1.5.10. \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed when \(P(X \in A) = P(Y \in A)\) for every set \(A\) of numbers. Theorem 1.5.10: that holds exactly when \(F_X(x) = F_Y(x)\) for every real \(x\).

How often heads equal tails. Toss a fair coin \(n\) times; \(X\) = heads, \(Y\) = tails. Swapping H and T in every outcome shows they're identically distributed for every \(n\).

Count agreements. \(X(s) = Y(s)\) means exactly \(n/2\) heads. With \(n = 2\): HT and TH, 2 of the 4 outcomes. With \(n = 3\): none, because 3 heads can't split evenly. Whether they ever agree depends on \(n\) being even, which has nothing to do with the definition.

Why one point isn't enough. \(X\) is uniform on \(\{1, 2, 3\}\) and \(Y\) is uniform on \(\{0, 2, 4\}\) (each value has probability \(\tfrac13\)). At \(x = 2\): \(F_X(2) = \tfrac23\) and \(F_Y(2) = \tfrac23\). Equal. But \(P(X = 1) = \tfrac13\) while \(P(Y = 1) = 0\), and \(F_X(0) = 0\) while \(F_Y(0) = \tfrac13\). Two cdfs that agree at one point can still describe different distributions.

Say it this way: "Identically distributed is a statement about probabilities: every event about \(X\) has the same probability as the same event about \(Y\)." Not this: "\(X\) and \(Y\) are the same variable" or "they never take the same value".

A fair coin is tossed six times. \(X\) = number of heads, \(Y\) = number of tails; they're identically distributed. On how many of the 64 equally likely outcomes is \(X(s) = Y(s)\)? (choose(n, k) is fine.)

\(X = Y\) means 3 heads and 3 tails: \(\binom63 = 20\) outcomes. So \(P(X = Y) = 20/64\): sometimes equal, sometimes not, and the definition says nothing either way.

\(X\) is uniform on \(\{1, 2, 3, 4\}\) and \(Y\) is uniform on \(\{0, 2, 3, 5\}\) (each value has probability \(\tfrac14\)), and \(F_X(3) = F_Y(3) = \tfrac34\). Are \(X\) and \(Y\) identically distributed?

Equal cdfs at every \(x\) are needed, and \(F_X(0) = 0 \ne \tfrac14 = F_Y(0)\). Equivalently \(P(X = 1) = \tfrac14\) but \(P(Y = 1) = 0\). \(P(X = Y)\) plays no part in the definition, and the definition isn't checked one \(x\) at a time: it's about every set \(A\).

\(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed. Sort each statement.

The first two are statements about probabilities, which the definition fixes (the second is the first at \(x = 3\)). The last two are about the functions' values outcome by outcome: three tosses' heads and tails are never equal, and six tosses' are equal only 20 times out of 64.

Part 3 · The chapter check (about 20 minutes)

From the reading: all of Chapter 1, §1.1–1.6. One or two questions per section, then one proof. Work them without the book. If you reach for the book, or guess, say so when the page asks.

§1.1 Sets

\(S = \{1, 2, \dots, 12\}\). \(A\) = the multiples of 3 in \(S\); \(B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}\). How many elements are in \(A^c \cap B^c\)?

\(A^c \cap B^c = (A \cup B)^c\) (De Morgan). \(A \cup B = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 12\}\), 8 elements, so its complement \(\{7, 8, 10, 11\}\) has 4.

§1.2 Axioms, rules and counting

State Kolmogorov's three axioms.

For every event \(A\): (1) \(P(A) \ge 0\); (2) \(P(S) = 1\); (3) if \(A_1, A_2, \dots\) are pairwise disjoint, \(P(\bigcup_i A_i) = \sum_i P(A_i)\).

A 4-digit PIN uses the digits 0–9, and no digit may appear twice. How many PINs are possible? (An expression such as 10*9*... is fine.)

Ordered, without replacement: \(10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7 = 5040\).

§1.3 Conditional probability and independence

Two fair dice are rolled. Given that at least one die shows a 6, what is the probability that the sum is 8? (A fraction is fine.)

At least one 6: \(6 + 6 - 1 = 11\) equally likely outcomes. Sum 8 among them: \((2, 6)\) and \((6, 2)\). So \(2/11\).

A disease affects 2% of a population. A test is positive for 90% of people who have it and for 5% of people who don't. A randomly chosen person tests positive. What is the probability they have the disease? (As a decimal to three places, or an expression.)

Bayes' rule with the partition {disease, no disease}: \(\dfrac{0.9 \times 0.02}{0.9 \times 0.02 + 0.05 \times 0.98} = \dfrac{0.018}{0.067} \approx 0.269\). Most positives are false positives, because the healthy group is so much bigger.

Casella & Berger, Exercise 1.39. Events \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, and \(P(A) > 0\) and \(P(B) > 0\). Prove that \(A\) and \(B\) are not independent. Name each fact you use.

Full marks: \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) (disjoint), so \(P(A \cap B) = P(\emptyset) = 0\) (Theorem 1.2.8a); but \(P(A)P(B) > 0\) (product of two positive numbers); so \(P(A \cap B) \ne P(A)P(B)\), and by the definition of independence (Definition 1.3.7) they are not independent. Got it: the argument is right with a citation missing. Not yet: argues from "disjoint events can't happen together" in words without comparing \(P(A \cap B)\) with \(P(A)P(B)\), or doesn't use the positivity of both probabilities.

\(P(A \cap B) = P(\emptyset) = 0\) (disjoint; Theorem 1.2.8a), while \(P(A)P(B) > 0\) since both factors are positive. The product rule fails, so \(A\) and \(B\) aren't independent. In words: learning \(A\) happened drops the probability of \(B\) from \(P(B) > 0\) to 0.

§1.4 Random variables

A fair coin is tossed four times, and \(X\) = the number of heads. Using the induced probability \(P_X(X \in A) = P(\{s : X(s) \in A\})\), find \(P(X \ge 3)\). (A fraction is fine.)

\(\{s : X(s) \ge 3\}\) is HHHH plus the four outcomes with one tail: 5 of 16 equally likely outcomes, so \(5/16\).

§1.5 Distribution functions

\(X\) has cdf \(F(x) = 1 - e^{-2x}\) for \(x \ge 0\) (and 0 for \(x < 0\)). Find \(P(0.5 < X \le 1)\). (Type exp(-1) for \(e^{-1}\); a decimal to three places is fine too.)

\(P(0.5 < X \le 1) = F(1) - F(0.5) = (1 - e^{-2}) - (1 - e^{-1}) = e^{-1} - e^{-2} \approx 0.233\).

§1.6 Densities and mass functions

\(f(x) = c\,x^2\) for \(0 \le x \le 2\) and 0 elsewhere. What value of \(c\) makes \(f\) a pdf?

\(\int_0^2 c\,x^2\,dx = c \cdot \tfrac83 = 1\), so \(c = \tfrac38\). (Condition (a), \(f \ge 0\), holds for any \(c > 0\).)

That's Chapter 1. Next comes Chapter 2: transformations of random variables and expected values, starting with its pretest.

Extra practice (optional)

From Casella & Berger, Chapter 1 exercises (worked solutions are in the Casella & Berger solutions manual):

  1. Exercise 1.47, if you skipped it after lesson 8: show that each of the given functions is a cdf, using Theorem 1.5.3.
  2. The tent density: \(f(x) = 4x\) on \([0, \tfrac12]\), \(4(1 - x)\) on \((\tfrac12, 1]\), 0 elsewhere. Check it's a pdf, find its cdf \(F(x)\) piece by piece, and confirm \(F\) has the three cdf properties.

Extra reading: John Haigh, Probability: A Very Short Introduction, Chapter 4, the section "Continuous distributions" (a few pages, in your library). A short, nontechnical take on describing a continuous quantity, a different angle from Casella & Berger's.

Extra article: "Dirac delta function", Wikipedia: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirac_delta_function>. Take Part 1's rectangle and let its width shrink to 0: the height grows without bound while the area stays 1. Dirac named that limit and made it popular (1927), and the article's probability section shows how it lets a discrete distribution be written as if it had a density, which joins the pmf and pdf halves of §1.6.
